h1: Carry-On ratings: what its critic and IMDb numbers mean
description: Carry-On has IMDb {{imdb}} and Rotten Tomatoes {{rt}} in this dated Netflix film dataset. Read the critic-score gap, voting context and limits.
summary: Carry-On has an IMDb rating of {{imdb}} and a Rotten Tomatoes Tomatometer of {{rt}}. In this arithmetic comparison, critics score higher than audiences by {{gapAbs}} points, a wide gap. The percentage counts positive reviews; IMDb averages viewer ratings. Their distance does not measure a difference in enjoyment. Scores come from OMDb as of {{asOf}}.

sections.heading: What does the Carry-On score difference actually measure?
paragraphs: The Rotten Tomatoes percentage is sharply higher than the IMDb rating after the latter is multiplied by ten: {{rt}} against {{imdbX10}}, a wide gap of {{gapAbs}} points. That calculation puts the figures on matching numeric ranges without making their meanings equivalent. A positive-review percentage cannot reveal the average grade critics gave.

The Metascore of {{metascore}} offers a useful check on that distinction. Numerically, this weighted critic average sits nearer the scaled IMDb figure than the Tomatometer does. One reading is that a high share of approving reviews can coexist with more moderate grades. The aggregates do not establish which story details individual critics or viewers liked.

The audience number has {{votes}} IMDb votes behind it. That is a substantial recorded pool, though vote volume alone does not establish representativeness or explain the difference. Among the {{genreCount}} {{genre}} films in this dataset, the median difference is {{genreMedianGap}}, in the opposite direction to Carry-On; its absolute difference ranks {{gapRank}} across {{setSize}} films.

Use those comparisons to describe the snapshot, rather than diagnose the film's reception. The [guide to the two rating systems](/compare/imdb-vs-rotten-tomatoes) explains why an average user rating and a positive-review share should remain separate signals.

sections.heading: Who is in Carry-On and how did it chart?
paragraphs: The setup is a rookie airport screener coerced by an unknown man into waving a hazardous item past the checkpoint on Christmas Eve. {{director}} directed it, with Taron Egerton, Jason Bateman and Sofia Carson listed among the lead cast in OMDb.

The same dated record lists a PG-13 classification, {{runtime}} running time, and the genres {{genre}}, crime and thriller. Its awards field reads 7 nominations total. Those are database fields, not additional reporting about awards or a firsthand assessment of the film.

Netflix's data gives it a peak rank of {{peakRank}} and {{weeksInTop10}} weeks in the global Top 10. Its {{hours}} hours figure comes from the Most Popular list's initial release window, rather than a sum over those chart weeks; that puts it {{popularityRank}} in this selected set.

sections.heading: How should Carry-On ratings guide a viewing choice?
paragraphs: If you look for broad critic approval before choosing an {{genre}} thriller, the Rotten Tomatoes figure of {{rt}} is the relevant measure. If you prefer the audience's average star rating, read IMDb's {{imdb}} directly. Neither is a promise that the film will suit your preferences.

The Metascore of {{metascore}} supplies another critic aggregate, with a different calculation from the Tomatometer. Someone deciding between the figures can read individual reviews to find out which aspects matter to them; this dataset cannot answer that question from the totals alone.

The PG-13 classification and OMDb runtime of {{runtime}} offer practical context about the selection. They do not turn a numerical rating into a recommendation for a particular household, so check the applicable content advice before making that decision.

sections.heading: Does Carry-On popularity establish audience approval?
paragraphs: No. Netflix hours viewed measure accumulated viewing time, not a count of unique people, completed watches or positive votes. Repeated viewing can contribute hours too. A peak rank of {{peakRank}} therefore describes chart performance without explaining the IMDb rating or Rotten Tomatoes percentage.

Carry-On's {{hours}} hours and {{weeksInTop10}} chart weeks also describe different reporting windows in this dataset. Treat the popularity rank as a comparison under the hub's stated selection rule, and the scores as separately dated measures of response. Neither can identify why a viewer pressed play or what persuaded a critic.

faq.q: How wide is the Carry-On gap between critics and audiences?
faq.a: The Rotten Tomatoes percentage is {{rt}}, while the IMDb rating of {{imdb}} converts arithmetically to {{imdbX10}}. The resulting {{gapAbs}} points form a wide gap, with the critic percentage higher. It ranks {{gapRank}} by absolute distance among {{setSize}} films, but the two measures are not interchangeable grades.

faq.q: Does Carry-On have any listed awards or nominations?
faq.a: The OMDb record gives the awards text as 7 nominations total. This page makes no further awards claim, because nothing beyond that string is cited here. Anyone who wants a fuller history should check the awarding bodies directly, since each publishes its own complete lists.

faq.q: How popular was Carry-On in Netflix's Top 10 data?
faq.a: Its peak was rank {{peakRank}}, with {{weeksInTop10}} global Top 10 weeks in the committed Netflix snapshot. The popularity figure of {{hours}} hours is from the initial release window in Netflix's Most Popular list and ranks {{popularityRank}} in this set. It measures viewing time, not unique viewers or their approval.
